```
6 Define vector $\widetilde{A}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{N}$ by $\widetilde{A}^{(i)}[k]:=A[k]\cdot\omega^{ki}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ (and similarly define vectors $\widetilde{B}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{N},\widetilde{C}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2N-1}$ )
7 Define vector $A^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}^{N}$ by $A^{(i)}[k]:=A[k]\cdot\omega_{b}^{ki}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ (and similarly define vectors $B^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}^{N},C^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}^{2N-1}$ ) // Recall that we assume a large prime $p_{b}$ is given as stated in Assumption 1.
8 Compute vector $\widetilde{Z}^{(i)}\leftarrow h(\widetilde{A}^{(i)})\star_{p}h(\widetilde{B}^{(i)})-h(\widetilde{C}^{(i)})$ via FFT
9 Compute vector $Z^{(i)}\leftarrow h(A^{(i)})\star_{p}h(B^{(i)})-h(C^{(i)})$ via FFT
10 Initialize $R\leftarrow(0,\dots,0)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2N-1}$
11 for $k\in[p]$ do
12 $f(x)\leftarrow\textsc{RecoverBucket}\big(\{\widetilde{Z}^{(i)}[k]\}_{i=0}^{2s},\{Z^{(i)}[k]\}_{i=0}^{2s},k\big)$ , where $f(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{2N-2}f_{\ell}x^{\ell}\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a polynomial in sparse representation
13 $R\leftarrow R+(f_{0},\dots,f_{2N-2})$
14 for $i\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(R)$ do
15 if $|R[i]+C[i]|>\|A\|_{\infty}\|B\|_{\infty}t$ then $R[i]\leftarrow-C[i]$
16 return $R$

```

```
Input: Values $\widetilde{v}_{0},\dots,\widetilde{v}_{2s}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , $v_{0},\dots,v_{2s}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ and $k\in[p]$
1 Output: a polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ represented as a list of non-zero coefficients. For details see Lemma 3.1
2 Use Prony’s method over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ (Lemma 2.11) with degree bound $2N/p$ , sparsity bound $s$ and $\omega_{pm}=\omega^{p}$ to obtain $g(y)=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}b_{j}y^{e_{j}}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[y]$ such that $g((\omega^{p})^{i})=\widetilde{v}_{i}/\omega^{ki}$ for all $0\leq i\leq 2s$ .
3 if Lemma 2.11 failed to find such a $g(y)\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[y]$ then return $0$
4 Determine $a_{1},\dots,a_{s^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ such that polynomial $f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}a_{j}x^{p\cdot e_{j}+k}$ satisfies $v_{i}=f(\omega_{b}^{i})$ for all $0\leq i<s^{\prime}$ , by solving a linear system over $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ .
5 for $j\in[s^{\prime}]$ do
6 if $a_{j}\in[\lfloor p_{b}/2\rfloor]$ then $a^{\prime}_{j}\leftarrow a_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}$
7 else $a^{\prime}_{j}\leftarrow a_{j}-p_{b}\in\mathbb{Z}$
8 return $f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}a_{j}^{\prime}x^{p\cdot e_{j}+k}$

```

#### Recovering algorithm.

At the beginning of Algorithm 1, based on the sparsity parameter $m$ , we sample a random prime $p\in[m/\log\log m,2m/\log\log m]$ and hash the indices into $p$ buckets according to their remainders modulo $p$ . For $k\in[p]$ , we say bucket $k$ is bad, if there is at least one bad index $i$ such that $i\equiv_{p}k$ . The number of terms mapped to bucket $k$ is the number of indices $i$ where $(A\star B-C)[i]\neq 0$ and $i\equiv_{p}k$ . We say bucket $k$ is heavy if the bucket contains more than $s$ elements ( $s=\lceil c\cdot\log\log m\rceil$ where $c$ is the constant from Corollary 2.5); otherwise, the bucket is light.

#### Lemma 3.1.

If a bucket $k\in[p]$ is light and does not contain bad indices, Algorithm 2 (given inputs computed in Algorithm 1) returns $\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}(A\star B-C)[i]x^{i}$ , where $\mathcal{B}$ is the set of indices in the bucket; otherwise, Algorithm 2 returns an $s$ -sparse polynomial. The running time of each call of Algorithm 2 is $(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta$ , after an $O(t^{2-\varepsilon}(\log\log m)/m+m+\log\log\Delta)$ initial preprocessing.

#### Proof.

For a light bucket $k$ that does not contain bad indices, suppose the nonzero terms in it have indices $k+pE_{1},\ldots,k+pE_{s^{\prime}}$ for some $s^{\prime},E_{1},\ldots,E_{s^{\prime}}$ . Then it is straightforward to verify that $\widetilde{v}_{i}=\widetilde{Z}^{(i)}[k]=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}(A\star B-C)[k+pE_{j}]\cdot\omega^{(k+pE_{j})i}$ . Thus, $\widetilde{v}_{i}/\omega^{ki}=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}(A\star B-C)[k+pE_{j}]\cdot(\omega^{p})^{iE_{j}}$ (note that we can precompute $\omega^{-ki}$ for all $k\in[p],i\in[2s+1]$ in $O(ps)=O(m)$ time, after computing $\omega^{-1}$ via exponentiation in $O(\log q)=O(\log P_{0}+\log t)=O(\log t+\log\log\Delta)$ time). Since the bucket contains no bad indices, $(A\star B-C)[k+pE_{j}]\neq 0$ in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , so Prony’s method can successfully recover $e_{1},\ldots,e_{s^{\prime}}$ where $e_{j}=E_{j}$ for every $j=1,\ldots,s^{\prime}$ .

Then in Line 2, we are solving a linear system where the coefficient matrix is

$$ \begin{bmatrix}1&1&\cdots&1\\
\omega_{b}^{p\cdot e_{1}+k}&\omega_{b}^{p\cdot e_{2}+k}&\cdots&\omega_{b}^{p\cdot e_{s^{\prime}}+k}\\
&&\vdots&\\
(\omega_{b}^{p\cdot e_{1}+k})^{s^{\prime}-1}&(\omega_{b}^{p\cdot e_{2}+k})^{s^{\prime}-1}&\cdots&(\omega_{b}^{p\cdot e_{s^{\prime}}+k})^{s^{\prime}-1}\\
\end{bmatrix}, $$

which is a transposed Vandermonde matrix. As $\omega_{b}$ has multiplicative order at least $2N$ , $\omega_{b}^{p\cdot e_{1}+k}$ , $\omega_{b}^{p\cdot e_{2}+k}$ , $\ldots,\omega_{b}^{p\cdot e_{s^{\prime}}+k}$ are distinct, and thus the Vandermonde matrix is invertible. Thus, the linear system has a unique solution, so we must have $a_{j}\equiv_{p_{b}}(A\star B-C)[k+pe_{j}]$ . Finally, as $\|A\star B-C\|_{\infty}\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t\Delta)<p_{b}/2$ by picking $p_{b}$ large enough, the choices of $a_{j}^{\prime}$ ensure that $a_{j}^{\prime}=(A\star B-C)[k+pe_{j}]$ .

If the bucket is not light, or if it contains a bad index, the algorithm might return $0$ , or some erroneous polynomial, but the sparsity of the polynomial is at most $s$ .

The bottlenecks of the algorithm are

- • Prony’s method: it runs in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)\log(p_{0}\kappa)=(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta$ time (after $O(N/p)=O(t^{2-\varepsilon}\log\log m/m)$ preprocessing).

- • Linear system solving: it runs in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)=(\log\log t)^{O(1)}$ time.

∎

#### Lemma 3.2.

Given parameter $m$ and vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ and $C\in\mathbb{Z}^{2N-1}$ with coefficient bound $\|A\|_{\infty},\|B\|_{\infty},\|C\|_{\infty}\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t\Delta)$ , Algorithm 1 returns a random vector $R\in\mathbb{Z}^{2N-1}$ in

$$ \displaystyle O(t^{2-\varepsilon}(\log\log m)/m \displaystyle+m\log t+(\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0})\cdot\log\log m \displaystyle+m(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log\Delta) $$

time such that:

- • If $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}\leq m$ , then

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[\|A\star B-C-R\|_{0}]\leq 0.4\|A\star B-C\|_{0}. $$

- • $\|R+C\|_{\infty}\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t\Delta)$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 3.1, if a bucket is light and does not contain bad indices, then RecoverBucket can successfully return all terms in the bucket. Thus, the following are the only possibilities that $(A\star B-C-R)[i]\neq 0$ for some term $i$ :

- • $i$ is in a heavy bucket. By Corollary 2.5, the number of terms in heavy buckets is at most $0.1\|A\star B-C\|_{0}$ , with probability $0.9$ . This means that the expected number of terms in heavy buckets is $\leq 0.1\|A\star B-C\|_{0}\cdot 0.9+\|A\star B-C\|_{0}\cdot 0.1\leq 0.19\|A\star B-C\|_{0}$ .

- • $i$ is in a light bucket that contains a bad index. As shown earlier, the probability that each $i\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B-C)$ is bad is $O(\frac{1}{\log^{2}t})$ . Thus, the expected number of bad indices is $O(\frac{\|A\star B-C\|_{0}}{\log^{2}t})$ . Each bad index can cause at most $s$ terms $i$ to be in a light bucket containing a bad index. Thus, the expected number of indices $i$ in this case is $O(\frac{\|A\star B-C\|_{0}s}{\log^{2}t})\leq o(\|A\star B-C\|_{0})$ .

- • $i$ is among the terms that are erroneously returned by RecoverBucket. By the previous two cases, the expected number of buckets that can cause RecoverBucket to return erroneously is at most

$$ \frac{0.19\|A\star B-C\|_{0}}{s}+O(\frac{\|A\star B-C\|_{0}}{\log^{2}t})\leq\frac{0.2\|A\star B-C\|_{0}}{s}. $$

Each such bucket can cause $s$ terms to be erroneous, so the expected number of indices $i$ in this case is $\leq 0.2\|A\star B-C\|_{0}$ .

Summing over all the cases, we get the claimed bound $\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[\|A\star B-C-R\|_{0}]\leq 0.4\|A\star B-C\|_{0}$ .

Line 1 ensures that $\|R+C\|_{\infty}\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t\Delta)$ . Note that it does not increase $\|A\star B-C-R\|_{0}$ because when $|R[i]+C[i]|>\|A\|_{\infty}\|B\|_{\infty}t$ , $(A\star B-C-R)[i]$ cannot be $0$ , so the sparsity $\|A\star B-C-R\|_{0}$ cannot increase when we reset the value of $R[i]$ .

Finally, we analyze the running time of the algorithm. The bottlenecks of the algorithm are the following:

- • The for loop starting at Line 1: Preparing $A^{(i)},B^{(i)},C^{(i)},\widetilde{A}^{(i)},\widetilde{B}^{(i)},\widetilde{C}^{(i)}$ takes $O(\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0})$ time for each iteration of the for loop (using bulk exponentiation [20, Lemma 4.2]). The FFT on Line 1 is for multiplying two degree- $O(m/\log\log m)$ polynomials in $\mathbb{F}_{q}[x]$ ; separately consider two cases: – If $\kappa=1$ , then $q$ is the prime $p_{0}$ . In this case, we can simply use FFT over integers (i.e., the standard FFT over complex numbers and then round to integers) then modulo $p_{0}$ to compute it in $O(m\log m/\log\log m)$ time.1313 13 In this case, $p_{0}$ may have dependency on $\Delta$ and cannot be bounded by $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(m)$ , so Theorem 2.8 and Corollary 2.9 would be too expensive here. – Otherwise, $\kappa\geq 2$ , so $q\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ . Hence, we can use Corollary 2.9 to compute it in time $O(m/\log\log m\cdot\log q)=O(m\log t/\log\log m)$ . The FFT on Line 1 can be computed by FFT over integers then modulo $p_{b}$ in $O(m\log m/\log\log m)$ time. Thus, the total running time over all iterations is $O(m\log t+(\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0})\cdot\log\log m)$ .

- • Calling RecoverBucket in Line 1: By Lemma 3.1, after a preprocessing with time $O(t^{2-\varepsilon}(\log\log m)/m+m+\log\log\Delta)$ , each call to RecoverBucket takes $(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta$ time. Summing over all $k\in[p]$ gives the $m(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta$ bound.

Note that even if $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}>m$ , we can still halt the algorithm after its running time exceeds the claimed time bound, so the time bound always holds. ∎

#### Lemma 3.3.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ be a fixed constant. Given a parameter $t$ and two vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ with the promise that $N<t^{2-\varepsilon}$ , where $t\geq\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|A\star B\|_{0}$ , one can compute $A\star B$ in $O(t\log t+t(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log\Delta)$ expected time by a Monte Carlo algorithm with $0.9$ success probability, where $\Delta=\max\{\|A\|_{\infty},\|B\|_{\infty}\}$ .

#### Proof.

We repeatedly apply Lemma 3.2. Initially, we set $m_{0}=100t$ and $C_{0}=0$ . For the $i$ -th time, we call Lemma 3.2 with $m=m_{i-1}$ and $C=C_{i-1}$ . Afterwards, we set $m_{i}\leftarrow 0.8\cdot m_{i-1}$ and $C_{i}\leftarrow C_{i-1}+R$ , where $R$ is returned by Lemma 3.2. After we reach $m_{i}\leq 2t/\log^{2}t$ , we use Lemma 2.16 to compute $A\star B$ with $\delta=1/t$ .

First, suppose we always have $m_{i}\geq\|A\star B-C_{i}\|_{0}$ for every $i$ . Then the running time of all calls to Lemma 3.2 can be bounded as (up to constant factors)

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{m}\left(t^{2-\varepsilon}(\log\log m)/m+m\log t+(\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0})\cdot\log\log m\right. \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\left.+m(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log\Delta\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{m}\left(t^{1-\varepsilon}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)+m\log t+(\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|A\star B\|_{0}+m)\cdot\log\log t\right. \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\left.+m(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log\Delta\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle t\log t+t(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log\Delta. $$

Also, as $\|A\star B-C_{i}\|_{0}\leq m_{i}\leq 2t/\log^{2}t$ holds when calling Lemma 2.16, the conditions of Lemma 2.16 are satisfied. Thus, we will get the correct $A\star B$ with error probability $1/t$ . The running time of Lemma 2.16 is $O(\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0}+t)\cdot\log(1/\delta)\leq O(\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|A\star B\|_{0}+2t/\log^{2}t+t)\cdot\log(1/\delta)=O(t\log t)$ .

It remains to bound the probability that we always have $m_{i}\geq\|A\star B-C_{i}\|_{0}$ for every $i$ . Let $E_{i}$ be the event that for every $0\leq j<i$ , $m_{j}\geq\|A\star B-C_{j}\|_{0}$ . We will show

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}\biggl[\|A\star B-C_{i}\|_{0}\mid E_{i}\biggr]\leq 0.4^{i}\cdot t $$

by induction. For $i=0$ , $\|A\star B-C_{0}\|_{0}=\|A\star B\|_{0}\leq t$ , so the base case holds. Now consider $i>0$ . By induction, we have $\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}\biggl[\|A\star B-C_{i-1}\|_{0}\mid E_{i-1}\biggr]\leq 0.4^{i-1}\cdot t$ and note that $E_{i}=E_{i-1}\wedge(m_{i-1}\geq\|A\star B-C_{i-1}\|_{0})$ . Thus, we have $\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}\biggl[\|A\star B-C_{i-1}\|_{0}\mid E_{i}\biggr]\leq\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}\biggl[\|A\star B-C_{i-1}\|_{0}\mid E_{i-1}\biggr]\leq 0.4^{i-1}\cdot t$ . Since $E_{i}$ implies $m_{i-1}\geq\|A\star B-C_{i-1}\|_{0}$ , Lemma 3.2 implies

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}\biggl[\|A\star B-C_{i}\|_{0}\mid E_{i}\biggr]\leq 0.4\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}\biggl[\|A\star B-C_{i-1}\|_{0}\mid E_{i}\biggr]\leq 0.4^{i}\cdot t. $$

Finally, the probability that $m_{i}\geq\|A\star B-C_{i}\|_{0}$ for every $i$ is exactly $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[E_{\ell}]$ , where $\ell$ is the total number of times we call Lemma 3.2, which can be bounded as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[E_{\ell}] \displaystyle=1-\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[\neg E_{\ell}] \displaystyle=1-\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\biggl[\|A\star B-C_{i-1}\|_{0}>m_{i-1}\mid E_{i-1}\biggr]\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[E_{i-1}] \displaystyle\geq 1-\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\biggl[\|A\star B-C_{i-1}\|_{0}>m_{i-1}\mid E_{i-1}\biggr] \displaystyle\geq 1-\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}\Bigl[\|A\star B-C_{i-1}\|_{0}\mid E_{i-1}\Bigr]/m_{i-1} \displaystyle\geq 1-\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\frac{0.4^{i-1}\cdot t}{0.8^{i-1}\cdot 100t} \displaystyle\geq 0.99. $$

∎

Finally, it remains to remove the assumption that an upper bound of $t$ is given. We follow the strategy of [20, Section 9], by guessing $\widetilde{t}=2^{\nu}\cdot\max\{\|A\|_{0},\|B\|_{0}\}$ for $\nu=0,1,\ldots,\lceil\log t\rceil$ as an upper bound for $t$ in Lemma 3.3. Note that we can halt Lemma 3.3 after $O(\widetilde{t}\log\widetilde{t}+\widetilde{t}(\log\log\widetilde{t})^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta)$ steps, and each call to Lemma 3.3 would still have constant success probability, provided that $\widetilde{t}\geq t$ . In order to boost the success probability, we run Lemma 2.19 after each call to Lemma 3.3, and only stop if the check in Lemma 2.19 passes.

Let $\nu^{*}$ be the smallest $\nu$ such that $2^{\nu}\cdot\max\{\|A\|_{0},\|B\|_{0}\}\geq t$ . Because of Lemma 2.19, when $\nu<\nu^{*}$ , the algorithm does not stop with a wrong answer w.h.p., and the total time spent for these iterations is $O(t\log t+t(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta)$ . For each iteration $\nu\geq\nu^{*}$ , the algorithm terminates with constant probability, say $3/4$ . Thus, the probability that we still have not succeeded right before calling Lemma 2.19 with parameter $\widetilde{t}=\max\{\|A\|_{0},\|B\|_{0}\}\cdot 2^{\nu}$ is $\leq 1/4^{\nu-\nu^{*}}$ . Therefore, the expected running time is (up to constant factors)

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\nu\geq\nu^{*}}\frac{1}{4^{\nu-\nu^{*}}}\cdot\big(2^{\nu-\nu^{*}}\cdot t\log(2^{\nu-\nu^{*}}\cdot t) \displaystyle+2^{\nu-\nu^{*}}\cdot t(\log\log(2^{\nu-\nu^{*}}\cdot t))^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log\Delta\big) \displaystyle\leq\  \displaystyle t\log t+t(\log\log t)^{O(1)}\log\log\Delta+\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log\Delta. $$

The error probability of the algorithm is bounded by constant.

#### Remark 3.4.

By combining the algorithm in this section with a length reduction step from [20, Section 10], we get an alternative Monte Carlo algorithm for Sparse Nonnegative Convolution in $O(t\log t)$ time with constant success probability (when $\Delta$ is not too big), partly recovering the main result of [20].

The length reduction in [20] does not work for general convolution with possibly negative entries, because they use an almost-affine hash function in this step, which can cause a zero entry to be split into multiple nonzero entries. See [20, Section 3.3] for more details.

## 4 Las Vegas Sparse Nonnegative Convolution

Now we turn to sparse convolution with nonnegative input numbers. Let $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ be the sparse input vectors with nonnegative integer entries with $\|A\|_{\infty},\|B\|_{\infty}\leq\Delta$ . In this section, we give a Las Vegas algorithm for Sparse Nonnegative Convolution with expected time $O(t\log t)$ , where $t=\|A\star B\|_{0}$ , under Assumption 1 (that a large prime $p_{b}=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(N\Delta)$ is given). We will improve it to terminate in $O(t\log t)$ time with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ probability in Section 5.

The meat of the proof is in Section 4.1, where we use the sparsity test of Lemma 2.13 to design a Las Vegas algorithm under two additional assumptions:

- • $N\leq t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ .

- • We are given an auxiliary small input set $S_{0}$ purported to satisfy $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)\subseteq S_{0}$ .

Then, in Section 4.2, we use more-or-less standard techniques to lift these two assumptions:

- • Using the length-reduction techniques from [20, 21] based on hashing, we can reduce the general case to the $N\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ case, and then to the $N\leq t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ case.

- • The desired auxiliary set $S_{0}$ can be supplied by running a Monte Carlo Sparse Convolution algorithm (such as [20] or Remark 3.4) to compute $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ . This set $S_{0}$ may be incorrect with small non-zero probability, but the Las Vegas algorithm is guaranteed to detect such an error when it happens.

### 4.1 Algorithm for short vectors

In this subsection, we assume $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ for some $N\leq t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ . This assumption will be useful for controlling the time complexity in two different places of the proof:

- • The iterative peeling procedure decreases the sparsity of $A\star B-C$ at exponential speed, so it only takes $O(\log\log t)$ iterations before the sparsity $m$ drops to $m\leq t/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ , at which point we can finish the computation using Corollary 2.18.

- • Our implementation of the sparsity tests needs to perform arithmetic operations on integers of magnitude roughly $(N/p)^{\log\log t}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t\Delta)$ , where prime $p=\Theta(m/\log\log t)$ is chosen according to the current sparsity $m\in[t/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t,t]$ . Our assumption $N\leq t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ implies that these integers have magnitude bounded by $(\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t)^{\log\log t}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t\Delta)\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t\Delta)$ and hence fit into constant many machine words, allowing constant time arithmetic operations.

We choose an element $\omega_{b}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ with multiplicative order at least $2N$ . As described in Section 3.1, this can be done using baby-step giant-step in $O(\sqrt{N}\log N)=O(t)$ time.

Our main subroutine, RecoveryStepLasVegas, is described in Algorithm 3, and its properties are stated in Lemma 4.1. The parameter $m$ in this subroutine will always be upper bounded by our main parameter $t$ for the Sparse Convolution problem.

```
Input: Sparse vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ , $C\in\mathbb{N}^{2N-1}$ such that $A\star B\geq C$ , and a set $S\subseteq[2N-1]$ and a parameter $m$
1 Output: A sparse vector $R\in\mathbb{N}^{2N-1}$ and a set $S^{\prime}\subseteq[2N-1]$ , for details see Lemma 4.1
2 Let parameter $s=\lceil c\cdot\log\log m\rceil$ . // $c$ is the constant from Corollary 2.5
3 Sample a random prime $p\in[m/\log\log m,2m/\log\log m]$ and let $h(x)=x\bmod p$ . Repeat until the number of elements of $S$ hashed by $h$ into heavy buckets (i.e., of size $\geq s$ ) is at most $0.1m$ .
4 for $i\leftarrow 0,1,2,\dots,2s$ do
5 Compute vector $Y^{(i)}\in\mathbb{N}^{p}$ according to Eq. 7, where $Y^{(i)}_{k}$ is defined as $\lVert\partial^{i}V_{k}\rVert_{1}$ for $V_{k}\in\mathbb{N}^{\lfloor(2N-2-k)/p\rfloor+1}$ such that $V_{k}[j]=(A\star B-C)[jp+k]$ .
6 Define vector $A^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}^{N}$ by $A^{(i)}[k]:=A[k]\cdot\omega_{b}^{ki}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ (and similarly define vectors $B^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}^{N},C^{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}^{2N-1}$ )
7 Compute vector $Z^{(i)}\leftarrow h(A^{(i)})\star_{p}h(B^{(i)})-h(C^{(i)})$
8 Initialize $R\leftarrow(0,\dots,0)\in\mathbb{N}^{2N-1}$
9 Initialize $S^{\prime}\leftarrow S$
10 for $k\in[p]$ do
11 if $Y^{(0)}_{k},Y^{(1)}_{k},\dots,Y^{(2s)}_{k}$ pass the $<s$ -sparsity test (Lemma 2.13) then
12 $f(x)\leftarrow\textsc{RecoverBucketLasVegas}\big(\{Z^{(i)}[k]\}_{i=0}^{2s},\{e\in S:e\equiv_{p}k\}\big)$ , where $f(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{2N-2}f_{\ell}x^{\ell}\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a polynomial in sparse representation
13 if $f$ is nonnegative and is consistent with $Y^{(0)}_{k},Y^{(1)}_{k},\dots,Y^{(2s)}_{k}$ then
14 $R\leftarrow R+(f_{0},\dots,f_{2N-2})$
15 $S^{\prime}\leftarrow S^{\prime}\setminus\{e\in S^{\prime}:f_{e}\neq 0\}$
16 return $R,S^{\prime}$

```

```
Input: Values $v_{0},\dots,v_{2s}\in\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ and a set $S_{k}=\{e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{s^{\prime}}\}\subseteq[2N-1]$
1 Output: a polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ represented as a list of non-zero coefficients.
2 Determine $a_{1},\dots,a_{s^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that polynomial $f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}a_{j}x^{e_{j}}$ satisfies $v_{i}=f(\omega_{b}^{i})$ for all $0\leq i\leq 2s$ , by solving a linear system over $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ and then converting the answers from $\mathbb{F}_{p_{b}}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ .
3 if successfully found $a_{1},\dots,a_{s^{\prime}}$ then return $f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{s^{\prime}}a_{j}x^{e_{j}}$
4 else return $f(x)=0$

```

#### Lemma 4.1.

Given parameter $m$ and vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ , $C\in\mathbb{N}^{2N-1}$ where $N\leq m\log^{7}m$ and $A\star B\geq C$ , and an auxiliary set $S\subseteq[2N-1]$ of size $|S|\leq m$ , Algorithm 3 returns a random sparse vector $R\in\mathbb{N}^{2N-1}$ and $S^{\prime}\subseteq[2N-1]$ in $O(m\log m+(\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0})\cdot\log\log m)$ time with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(m)$ probability, such that:

- • $R\leq A\star B-C$ always holds.

- • If $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}\leq m$ and $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B-C)\subseteq S$ , then we always have

$$ \|A\star B-C-R\|_{0}\leq 0.1m\quad\text{ and }\quad\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B-C-R)\subseteq S^{\prime}. $$

#### Proof.

We first define $X^{(i)}$ , which will be used to compute $Y^{(i)}$ defined at Line 3: for $i\in\{0,1,\dots,2s\}$ , $X^{(i)}\in\mathbb{N}^{p}$ is defined by

$$ X^{(i)}:=\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i}\tbinom{i}{j}h(\partial^{j}A)\star_{p}h(\partial^{i-j}B)\Big)-h(\partial^{i}C), $$

so for $k\in[p]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle X^{(i)}_{k} \displaystyle=\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i}\tbinom{i}{j}\sum_{k^{\prime}\in[p]}\sum_{\ell_{1}\equiv_{p}k^{\prime}}(\ell_{1}^{j}A_{\ell_{1}})\sum_{\ell_{2}\equiv_{p}k-k^{\prime}}(\ell_{2}^{i-j}B_{\ell_{2}})\Big)-h(\partial^{i}C)_{k} \displaystyle=\Big(\sum_{k^{\prime}\in[p]}\sum_{\ell_{1}\equiv_{p}k^{\prime}}\sum_{\ell_{2}\equiv_{p}k-k^{\prime}}((\ell_{1}+\ell_{2})^{i}A_{\ell_{1}}B_{\ell_{2}})\Big)-h(\partial^{i}C)_{k} \displaystyle=\Big(\sum_{\ell\equiv_{p}k}\ell^{i}(A\star B)_{\ell}\Big)-h(\partial^{i}C)_{k} \displaystyle=h(\partial^{i}(A\star B-C))_{k}. $$

Therefore, by running the sparsity test of Lemma 2.13 using $X^{(0)}_{k},X^{(1)}_{k},\dots,X^{(2s)}_{k}$ , we would be able to verify whether the bucket $k$ has less than $s$ elements, but the time complexity would be too high, due to high-precision integers: The integers $X^{(i)}_{k}$ can have magnitude roughly as large as $\Delta m\cdot N^{2s}$ where $s=\Theta(\log\log m)$ , so computing them directly using FFT would lead to a $\log\log m$ factor blow up. That’s why we introduce $Y^{(i)}$ as an alternative: By definition of $Y^{(i)}$ at Line 3,

$$ Y^{(i)}_{k}=\sum_{d=0}^{\lfloor(2N-k-1)/p\rfloor}d^{i}\cdot(A\star B-C)[k+dp], $$

which is analogous to $X_{k}^{(i)}$ (in the sense that running the sparsity test of Lemma 2.13 on $Y^{(0)}_{k},Y^{(1)}_{k},\dots,Y^{(2s)}_{k}$ would also decide whether the bucket $k$ has less than $s$ elements), but has smaller magnitude and hence fits into constant many machine words of length $\Omega(\log m+\log\Delta)$ bits:

$$ \displaystyle 0\leq Y_{k}^{(i)} \displaystyle\leq(2N/p)^{i}\sum_{d=0}^{\lfloor(2N-k-1)/p\rfloor}(A\star B-C)[k+dp] \displaystyle\leq(\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log m)^{2s}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(m\Delta) \displaystyle\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(m\Delta), $$

where we used the assumption that $N\leq m\log^{7}m$ and that $p=\Theta(m/\log\log m),s=\Theta(\log\log m)$ . In the following we describe how to compute the integers $Y_{k}^{(i)}$ efficiently.

Note that $Y^{(i)}_{k}$ is determined by $\left\{X^{(j)}_{k}\right\}_{0\leq j\leq i}$ using the following recurrence:

$$ Y_{k}^{(i)}=p^{-i}\cdot\Big(X_{k}^{(i)}-\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}\tbinom{i}{j}k^{i-j}p^{j}Y_{k}^{(j)}\Big). $$

We compute all $X_{k}^{(i)}$ mod $M$ using FFTs over integers, where $M=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(m\Delta)$ is a power of $2$ that is larger than the upper bound in Eq. 6. More specifically, we compute the DFTs of $h(\partial^{i}A),h(\partial^{i}B)$ for all $0\leq i\leq 2s$ in $O(p\log p)\cdot 2s\leq O(m\log m)$ total time. Then, using the fact that the DFT of the convolution of two vectors is the entry-wise multiplication of their DFTs, by Eq. 5 we can compute the DFT of $X^{(i)}$ for all $0\leq i\leq 2s$ , in $O(s^{2}\cdot p)\leq O(m\log\log m)$ time. Finally, we perform inverse-DFT to recover all $X^{(i)}$ in $O(p\log p)\cdot 2s\leq O(m\log m)$ time.

Then, we use Eq. 7 to compute all $Y_{k}^{(i)}$ modulo $M$ in $p\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)\leq m\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(\log\log m)$ time. Note that we need to compute $p^{-1}$ in the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ (recall that we picked $M$ to be a power of $2$ , so $p^{-1}$ exists). We can do so in $O(p)$ time by finding the smallest $jM+1$ for $j<p$ that is divisible by $p$ , and $p^{-1}$ would be $\frac{jM+1}{p}$ . Since $M=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(m\Delta)$ is chosen to be large enough, we actually recover all $Y_{k}^{(i)}$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ .

When invoking Lemma 2.13 in Line 3 for the sparsity test, we need to compute the determinant of an $s\times s$ integer matrix where each entry fits into constant many machine words. This can be done using Theorem 2.7 in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(\log\log m)$ time. Then, checking whether $f$ is consistent with $Y_{k}^{(i)}$ (meaning that $Y^{(i)}_{k}=\sum_{d=0}^{\lfloor(2N-2-k)/p\rfloor}d^{i}\cdot f_{k+dp}$ where $f(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{2N-2}f_{\ell}x^{\ell}$ ) at Line 3 takes $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(s)=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(\log\log m)$ time.

The bottlenecks of the algorithm are the following:

- • The cost for finding a good $p$ . By Corollary 2.5, the number of terms in heavy buckets is at most $0.1|S|\leq 0.1m$ , with probability $\geq 0.9$ . This means that we only need to repeat $O(\log m)$ times to achieve high probability. Therefore, the running time is $O(m\log m)$ w.h.p.

- • The for loop starting at Line 3. The FFTs there take $O(s\cdot p\log p)=O(m\log m)$ time, and preparing the arrays $\partial^{i}A,\partial^{i}B,\partial^{i}C,A^{(i)},B^{(i)},C^{(i)}$ takes $O((\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0}+\|C\|_{0})\cdot\log\log m)$ time. The claimed time bound thus follows.

Finally, we verify the guarantees of the lemma.

- • $R\leq A\star B-C$ always holds. If the condition on Line 3 is satisfied, then we know that there are less than $s$ terms in bucket $k$ . By Lemma 2.14, the only $s$ -sparse nonnegative polynomial $f$ that is consistent with $X_{k}^{(i)}$ (i.e., $\|\partial^{i}f\|_{1}=X_{k}^{(i)}$ ) is the one containing the correct terms in the bucket $k$ . Consequently, the only $s$ -sparse polynomial $f$ whose nonzero terms all have indices consistent with $Y_{k}^{(i)}$ is the one containing the correct terms in the bucket $k$ . Thus, if the algorithm passes the condition on Line 3, we know $f_{\ell}=(A\star B-C)_{\ell}$ for all $\ell\equiv_{p}k$ , and by RecoverBucketLasVegas, $f_{\ell}=0$ for all $\ell\not\equiv_{p}k$ . Therefore, $R\leq A\star B-C$ always holds.

- • If $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B-C)\subseteq S$ , then $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B-C-R)\subseteq S^{\prime}$ . This is implied by the same analysis as above.

- • If $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}\leq m$ and $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B-C)\subseteq S$ , then Algorithm 3 recovers all items in light buckets. As $p$ is a good prime, $\|A\star B-C-R\|_{0}\leq 0.1m$ .∎

#### Lemma 4.2.

Given vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ , a parameter $t$ where $N\leq t\log^{5}t$ , and an auxiliary set $S_{0}\subseteq[2N-1]$ of size $|S_{0}|\leq t$ , there is a randomized algorithm in (worst case) $O(t\log t)$ time that outputs either a sparse vector or $\bot$ , with the following guarantee:

- • Either $output=A\star B$ or $output=\bot$ (always).

- • If $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)\subseteq S_{0}$ , then $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[output=\bot]\leq 1/t$ .

Note that the failure probability can be reduced to $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ by a constant number of repetitions.

#### Proof.

We repeatedly apply Lemma 4.1, starting with parameters $m_{0}=t,C_{0}=0,S_{0}$ and continuing with $m_{i+1}=0.1\cdot m_{i},C_{i+1}=C_{i}+R,S_{i+1}=S^{\prime}$ , until we reach $m_{i}\leq t/\log^{2}t$ . If $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)\subseteq S_{0}$ , then by induction we can show $\|A\star B-C_{i}\|_{0}\leq m_{i}\leq t/\log^{2}t$ . Then, we run Corollary 2.18 using $C_{i}$ to compute $C=A\star B$ . By the guarantees of Lemma 4.1 and Corollary 2.18, we always have $C\leq A\star B$ , we can check whether $C=A\star B$ by verifying whether $\lVert C\rVert_{1}=\lVert A\rVert_{1}\lVert B\rVert_{1}$ . If $C\neq A\star B$ , then some call to Lemma 4.1 or Corollary 2.18 failed, which happens with probability at most $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ .

The total running time for calling Lemma 4.1 is

$$ \sum_{m_{i}}O(m_{i}\log t+t\log\log m)=O(t\log t+t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log\log t), $$

as $m_{i}$ is geometrically decreasing and the number of them is $O(\log\log t)$ . The running time of Corollary 2.18 is

$$ O(t\log N+(t/\log^{2}t)\log^{2}N(\log(t/\log^{2}t)+\log\log N))=O(t\log t). $$

Note that the guarantees of Lemma 4.1 and Corollary 2.18 ensure that we never return an incorrect vector, even if $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)\not\subseteq S_{0}$ . ∎

### 4.2 Length reduction

To relax the $N\leq t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ assumption in the previous subsection, we first need to reduce the length of the input vectors from $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ to $t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ by hashing modulo a random prime $p\leq t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log t$ . This length reduction is similar to [20, Section 7], and can be additionally made Las Vegas using the techniques from [21, Section 4.5]. Using this reduction, we prove the following lemma:

#### Lemma 4.3.

Given vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ where $N\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(\|A\|_{0}\|B\|_{0})$ , and a parameter $t\geq\|A\star B\|_{0}$ , there is a Las Vegas algorithm that returns $C=A\star B$ in expected $O(t\log t)$ time. Even when $t<\|A\star B\|_{0}$ , the algorithm is Las Vegas.

#### Proof.

Let $p$ be a random prime from $[0.5t\log^{5}t,t\log^{5}t]$ and let $h(x)=x\bmod p$ , which hashes the terms in $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ into $p$ buckets. Compute $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ by an $O(t\log t)$ -time Monte Carlo algorithm with constant success probability (such as the algorithm in Theorem 1.3). Then, using the computed $S_{0}=\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ , we use Lemma 4.2 to compute $V^{(0)}=h(A)\star_{p}h(B)=h(A\star B)$ , and similarly compute $V^{(1)}=h(\partial A)\star_{p}h(B)+h(A)\star_{p}h(\partial B)=h(\partial(A\star B))$ and $V^{(2)}=h(\partial^{2}A)\star_{p}h(B)+2h(\partial A)\star_{p}h(\partial B)+h(A)\star_{p}h(\partial^{2}B)=h(\partial^{2}(A\star B))$ , in $O(t\log t)$ time (with failure probability $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ ). Here we remark that, since Lemma 4.2 only takes non-cyclic vectors instead of cyclic vectors (with indices modulo $p$ ) as input, we need to first view these cyclic input vectors as non-cyclic ones, and use $\{i\in[2p-1]:i\bmod p\in S_{0}\}$ as the auxiliary set supplied to Lemma 4.2; the output vectors of Lemma 4.2 are then hashed back to cyclic vectors under $h(x)=x\bmod p$ .

Then for every $k\in[p]$ , we use the values $V^{(0)}[k],V^{(1)}[k],V^{(2)}[k]$ to perform a sparsity test (Lemma 2.13) to check whether bucket $k$ contains a unique term in $O(1)$ time. If the check passes, we can use $V^{(1)}[k]/V^{(0)}[k]$ to recover the index of the term, and use $V^{(0)}[k]$ to recover the value of the term.

As $p$ is a random prime from $[0.5t\log^{5}t,t\log^{5}t]$ , for each fixed $i\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ , the probability that $i$ collides with some other term in a bucket is $O(t\cdot\frac{\log N/\log(t\log^{5}t)}{t\log^{5}t/\log(t\log^{5}t)})=O(1/\log^{4}t)$ by the prime number theorem (similarly to Footnote 2). Therefore, the expected number of indices that collide is $O(t/\log^{4}t)$ , so by Markov’s inequality, with constant probability, we have recovered all but $O(t/\log^{4}t)$ indices. Then we use Corollary 2.18 to correct the remaining $O(t/\log^{4}t)$ errors and compute $A\star B$ in $O(t\log t)$ time (with failure probability $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ ).

Similarly as before, we always have $C\leq A\star B$ , so by verifying whether $\|A\|_{1}\|B\|_{1}=\|C\|_{1}$ , we can check whether $A\star B=C$ . If $\|A\|_{1}\|B\|_{1}\neq\|C\|_{1}$ , we return $\bot$ . ∎

Lemma 4.3 requires knowing a good upper bound on $\|A\star B\|_{0}$ . To relax this requirement, we could again use the exponential guessing strategy of [20, Section 9] (which we used in the end of Section 3 for our sparse general convolution algorithm). But here we can use the simpler method by Fischer [42] based on nonnegativity of $A,B$ : we apply Lemma 2.15 to obtain a constant approximation of $t=\|A\star B\|_{0}=|\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A)+\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(B)|$ in $O(t\log t)$ time (with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ success probability), and then run Lemma 4.3 using this upper bound. Then we immediately get the following corollary:

#### Corollary 4.4.

Given vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ where $N\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(\|A\|_{0}\|B\|_{0})$ , there is a Las Vegas algorithm that returns $C=A\star B$ in expected $O(t\log t)$ time, where $t=\|A\star B\|_{0}$ .

Finally we relax the $N\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ requirement by another length reduction step in [21, Section 4.5] based on almost linear hash functions $h\colon[N]\to[\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)]$ ([21, Lemma 13]). This is summarized in the following lemma:

#### Lemma 4.5 (Length reduction from $N$ to $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ , [21, Section 4.5]).

Suppose there is a Las Vegas algorithm for computing $A\star B$ , where $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ and $N\leq(\|A\|_{0}\|B\|_{0})^{3}$ , which terminates in $T(\|A\star B\|_{0})$ time with $\geq 1-\delta$ probability.

Then, there is a Las Vegas algorithm for computing $A\star B$ , where $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ , which terminates in $O(T(\|A\star B\|_{0}))$ time with $\geq 1-\delta-1/\|A\star B\|_{0}^{5}$ probability.

By combining Lemma 4.5 and Corollary 4.4, we immediately obtain a Las Vegas algorithm for computing $A\star B$ in expected $O(t\log t)$ time, where $t=\|A\star B\|_{0}$ .

## 5 Achieving High Success Probability

The Las Vegas algorithm for Sparse Nonnegative Convolution described in Section 4 terminates in $O(t\log t)$ time only with $0.9$ probability (by Markov’s inequality). In this section, we will boost this probability to $1-1/t$ , thereby proving our main Theorem 1.1 under Assumption 1 (which will be removed in Appendix A).

Throughout this section, we assume the main parameter $t$ is large enough in order to simplify some calculations.

### 5.1 Estimating supports via sparse convolution modulo small prime

Our algorithm with high success probability crucially relies on the following lemma for computing sparse convolution $A\star B$ given $A,B\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{N}$ where both $N$ and prime $q$ are small. Here we measure sparsity $t$ by the size of the sumset $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A)+\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(B)$ (also called “structural support” in [8, 78]), which may be larger than the actual support $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ due to vanishing over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ . In the dense regime $t=\Theta(N)$ , the time complexity matches the $O(N\log q)$ bound in Theorem 2.8.

#### Lemma 5.1 (Computing $A\star B$ modulo small prime for short vectors).

Let $t$ be a parameter, $N\leq t\log^{5}t$ , and $q\in[0.5\log^{25}t,\log^{25}t]$ be a prime. Given sparse vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{N}$ , there is a randomized algorithm in (worst case) $O(t\log\log t)$ time that outputs either a vector in $\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2N-1}$ or $\bot$ , with the following guarantee:

- • If $|\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A)+\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(B)|\leq t$ , then $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[\text{output}=\bot]\leq 1/\log t$ .

- • $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\big[\text{output}\neq\bot\text{ and }\text{output}\neq A\star B\big]\leq 1/t$ .

Note that in Lemma 5.1 we can assume without loss of generality that the input vectors have sparsity $|\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A)|,|\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(B)|\leq t$ ; otherwise, it is always valid to output $\bot$ . (This assumption also applies to the upcoming Lemma 5.2 and Lemma 5.4.)

Lemma 5.1 is slightly weaker than a Las Vegas algorithm: it reports failure with moderately low probability, and outputs a wrong answer with inverse-polynomial probability. Nevertheless, Lemma 5.1 is used as a subroutine in our main Las Vegas algorithm (Theorem 1.1).

Lemma 5.1 is proved by a vast modification and refinement of [20]; we defer its proof to Section 5.3. In the following, we show two applications of Lemma 5.1, which are used later in Section 5.2 to obtain the desired high-probability Las Vegas algorithm for Sparse Nonnegative Convolution.

As a first application of Lemma 5.1, we give a very fast algorithm that accurately estimates the support size of (cyclic) sparse nonnegative convolution:

#### Lemma 5.2 (Estimating $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}$ for small $p$ ).

Let $t$ be a parameter, and prime $p\leq t\log^{5}t$ . Given nonnegative sparse vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{p}$ , there is a randomized algorithm in (worst case) $O(t\log\log t)$ time that outputs either an integer or $\bot$ , with the following guarantee:

- • If $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\leq t$ , then $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[\text{output}=\bot]\leq 1/\log t$ .

- • $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\Big[\text{output}\neq\bot\text{ and }\big\lvert\text{output}-\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\big\rvert\geq\sqrt{\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}}t^{0.4}\Big]\leq 1/\sqrt{t}$ .

A natural idea to prove Lemma 5.2 is as follows: replace the positive entries of $A,B$ by random $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -elements where $q=\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ , and invoke Lemma 5.1 to compute their convolution. Then we expect roughly $1-1/q$ fraction of $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ to survive in the convolution result. We slightly modify this idea in the following proof to make the analysis easier.

#### Proof of Lemma 5.2.

Assume $A,B\in\{0,1\}^{p}$ without loss of generality, as replacing the positive entries by ones does not change $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ . Pick an arbitrary prime $q\in[0.5\log^{25}(8t),\log^{25}(8t)]$ . Define random vectors $\hat{A},\hat{B}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{3p}$ as follows:

- • For $0\leq i<p$ , let $\hat{A}[i]=\begin{cases}\text{a random element $\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$}&A[i]=1,\\ 0&A[i]=0.\end{cases}$

- • For $0\leq i<p$ , let $\hat{B}[i]=\begin{cases}\text{a random element $\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$}&B[i]=1,\\ 0&B[i]=0.\end{cases}$

- • For $0\leq i<p$ , let $\hat{A}[i+2p]=A[i]\in\{0,1\}$ .

- • For $0\leq i<p$ , let $\hat{B}[i+2p]=B[i]\in\{0,1\}$ .

- • All other unspecified coordinates in $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ are zeros.

Let $\hat{C}=\hat{A}\star\hat{B}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{6p-1}$ . We can verify that $|\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(\hat{A})+\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(\hat{B})|\leq 3\|A\star B\|_{0}\leq 6\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}$ . Moreover, the middle part of $\hat{C}$ encodes the information of $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ in the following sense: For every $k\in[p]$ , we can verify that

$$ \displaystyle\hat{C}[k+2p]+\hat{C}[k+3p]=\begin{cases}0&(A\star_{p}B)[k]=0,\\
\sum_{i+j\equiv_{p}k,\,A[i]=B[j]=1}(\hat{A}[i]+\hat{B}[j])&(A\star_{p}B)[k]>0.\end{cases} $$

Note that we included both $\hat{C}[k+2p]$ and $\hat{C}[k+3p]$ to take care of the wrap-around of $i+j$ modulo $p$ . As we can see, in the $(A\star_{p}B)[k]>0$ case, the result of $\hat{C}[k+2p]+\hat{C}[k+3p]$ is the sum of (at least one) independent uniformly random $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -elements, and hence vanishes with exactly $1/q$ probability. Hence, the sum of indicators

$$ S:=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\mathbf{1}\big[\hat{C}[k+2p]+\hat{C}[k+3p]\neq 0\big] $$

has expectation $\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[S]=(1-1/q)\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}$ . Moreover, we can analyze the concentration of $S$ using the following claim.

#### Claim 5.3.

Assume $A,B\in\{0,1\}^{p}$ are not both all- $1$ vectors. For every distinct $k,k^{\prime}\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ , the random variables $\hat{C}[k+2p]+\hat{C}[k+3p]$ and $\hat{C}[k^{\prime}+2p]+\hat{C}[k^{\prime}+3p]$ are pairwise independent.

Note that if the assumption in Claim 5.3 does not hold, then $A\star_{p}B$ is the all- $p$ vector, and we can immediately finish by outputting $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}=p$ .

#### Proof of Claim 5.3.

Denote $c_{k}=\hat{C}[k+2p]+\hat{C}[k+3p]$ for short. By Eq. 8, both $c_{k}$ and $c_{k^{\prime}}$ are sums of independent uniformly random $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -elements, where the summands for $c_{k}$ and for $c_{k^{\prime}}$ may be overlapping. In more detail, let $I_{k}:=\{i\in[p]:A[i]=B[(k-i)\bmod p]=1\}$ and $J_{k}:=\{j\in[p]:B[j]=A[(k-j)\bmod p]=1\}$ . Then, by definition, $c_{k}$ equals the sum of random $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -elements, $\sum_{i\in I_{k}}\hat{A}[i]+\sum_{j\in J_{k}}\hat{B}[j]$ , and similarly for $c_{k^{\prime}}$ . In order to show $c_{k}$ and $c_{k^{\prime}}$ are pairwise independent, it suffices to show that these two sets of summands are not identical, that is, we want to show either $I_{k}\neq I_{k^{\prime}}$ or $J_{k}\neq J_{k^{\prime}}$ .

To show this, simply note that $|I_{k}|=|J_{k}|$ and $\sum_{i\in I_{k}}i+\sum_{j\in J_{k}}j\equiv_{p}k\cdot|I_{k}|$ , and similar equations hold for $k^{\prime}$ . Suppose to the contrary that $(I_{k},J_{k})=(I_{k^{\prime}},J_{k^{\prime}})$ . Then $|I_{k}|=|I_{k^{\prime}}|$ , and the previous property implies $k\cdot|I_{k}|\equiv_{p}k^{\prime}\cdot|I_{k^{\prime}}|$ . Note that $|I_{k}|,|I_{k^{\prime}}|\geq 1$ since $k,k^{\prime}\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ . If $|I_{k}|<p$ , then by division modulo prime $p$ we obtain $k\equiv_{p}k^{\prime}$ , contradicting the assumption that $k\neq k^{\prime}$ . If $|I_{k}|=p$ , then it must hold that both $A,B\in\{0,1\}^{p}$ are all- $1$ vectors, which violates the initial assumption. ∎

From Claim 5.3, we know the random variable $S$ defined in Eq. 9 has variance $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Var}}[S]=\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\cdot(1/q)(1-1/q)$ . By Chebyshev’s inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\left[\,|S-\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[S]|\geq(1-1/q)\sqrt{\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}}t^{0.3}\right] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{\operatorname*{\mathbf{Var}}[S]}{\big((1-1/q)\sqrt{\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}}t^{0.3}\big)^{2}}=\frac{1}{(q-1)t^{0.6}}. $$

Define estimator $\widetilde{S}:=qS/(q-1)$ which has expectation $\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[\widetilde{S}]=q\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[S]/(q-1)=\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}$ . By scaling both sides of $|S-\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}[S]|\geq(1-1/q)\sqrt{\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}}t^{0.3}$ by $q/(q-1)$ , the previous inequality implies

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\big[\big\lvert\widetilde{S}-\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\big\rvert\geq\sqrt{\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}}t^{0.3}\big]\leq\frac{1}{(q-1)t^{0.6}}<1/t^{0.6}. $$

Now we continue to describe our algorithm: We apply the randomized algorithm from Lemma 5.1 to $\hat{A},\hat{B}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{3p}$ with parameter $8t$ , which terminates in $O(t\log\log t)$ time. If Lemma 5.1 returns $\bot$ , then we return $\bot$ . Otherwise, let $\widetilde{C}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{6p-1}$ be returned by Lemma 5.1, and we return $\frac{q}{q-1}\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\mathbf{1}\big[\widetilde{C}[k+2p]+\widetilde{C}[k+3p]\neq 0\big]$ , rounded to the nearest integer.

Now we analyze the correctness of this algorithm. First, if $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\leq t$ , then $|\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(\hat{A})+\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(\hat{B})|\leq 8\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\leq 8t$ , and by Lemma 5.1 we know the probability of returning $\bot$ is at most $1/\log(8t)\leq 1/\log(t)$ , as desired. Second, the probability that Lemma 5.1 returns $\widetilde{C}$ but $\widetilde{C}\neq\hat{A}\star\hat{B}=\hat{C}$ is at most $1/(8t)$ . In the successful case where $\widetilde{C}=\hat{C}$ , the integer we return is $\widetilde{S}$ (up to additive difference 1 due to rounding), and by Eq. 10 we know the probability that it differs from $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}$ by at least $\sqrt{\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}}t^{0.4}>\sqrt{\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}}t^{0.3}+1$ is no more than $1/t^{0.6}$ . By a union bound, the overall error probability is at most $1/(8t)+1/t^{0.6}\leq 1/\sqrt{t}$ as desired. This finishes the proof of correctness of Lemma 5.2. ∎

By a similar proof to the above, we can also use Lemma 5.1 to compute $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ given $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{p}$ with high probability of correctness, as stated in the following lemma:

#### Lemma 5.4 (Computing $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ for small $p$ w.h.p.).

Let $t$ be a parameter, and prime $p\leq t\log^{5}t$ . Given sparse vectors $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{p}$ , there is a randomized algorithm in (worst case) $O(t\log t)$ time that outputs either a subset of $[p]$ or $\bot$ , with the following guarantee:

- • If $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\leq t$ , then $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[\text{output}=\bot]\leq 1/t^{2}$ .

- • $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}\big[\text{output}\neq\bot\text{ and }\text{output}\neq\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)\big]\leq 1/\sqrt{t}$ .

#### Proof.

Again, we assume without loss of generality that $A,B\in\{0,1\}^{p}$ . Our algorithm has $\ell:=\lceil 10\log t/\log\log t\rceil$ independent rounds, each with worst case time complexity $O(t\log\log t)$ . The total time complexity is thus $O(t\log t)$ .

Pick an arbitrary prime $q\in[0.5\log^{25}(8t),\log^{25}(8t)]$ . In the $r$ -th round ( $r\in[\ell]$ ), we construct random vectors $\hat{A}^{(r)},\hat{B}^{(r)}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{3p}$ , and apply Lemma 5.1 to $\hat{A}^{(r)},\hat{B}^{(r)}$ with parameter $8t$ , in the same way as in the proof of Lemma 5.2. We denote $\hat{C}^{(r)}=\hat{A}^{(r)}\star\hat{B}^{(r)}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{6p-1}$ , and we denote the output of Lemma 5.1 by $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}$ , which is either $\bot$ or a vector in $\mathbb{F}_{q}^{6p-1}$ . Recall from Eq. 8 that for each $k\in[p]$ , $\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+2p]+\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+3p]$ is a random $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -element if $(A\star_{p}B)[k]\neq 0$ , and zero otherwise.

After all $\ell$ rounds are finished:

- • If more than $\ell/3$ rounds returned $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}=\bot$ , then we return $\bot$ .

- • Otherwise, we return the set

$$ \{k\in[p]:\text{exists }r\in[\ell]\text{ s.t. }\widetilde{C}^{(r)}\neq\bot\text{ and }\widetilde{C}^{(r)}[k+2p]+\widetilde{C}^{(r)}[k+3p]\neq 0\}. $$

(11)

To analyze the correctness of this algorithm, we need the following three claims. Recall that we assume $t$ is large enough in order to simplify calculations.

#### Claim 5.5.

With at least $1-1/t^{18}$ probability, for every $k\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ , the number of $r\in[\ell]$ such that $\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+2p]+\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+3p]\neq 0$ is at least $\ell/2$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $k\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ . Since the $\ell$ rounds are independent, and in each round $\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+2p]+\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+3p]$ is a random $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -element, the probability that more than $\ell/2$ of them are zeros is at most

$$ \binom{\ell}{\ell/2}\cdot(1/q)^{\ell/2}<(4/q)^{\ell/2}<\left(\frac{4}{0.5\log^{25}(8t)}\right)^{5\log t/\log\log t}\leq\frac{1}{t^{20}}. $$

We apply a union bound over at most $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\leq p\leq t\log^{5}t$ many $k$ ’s, and the total failure probability is at most $1/t^{18}$ . ∎

#### Claim 5.6.

Suppose $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\leq t$ . Then, with at least $1-1/t^{2}$ probability, the number of rounds $r$ with $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}=\bot$ is at most $\ell/3$ .

#### Proof.

If $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\leq t$ , then, similarly to the argument in the proof of Lemma 5.2, we know each round returns $\bot$ with at most $1/\log(8t)$ probability as guaranteed by Lemma 5.1. Then the probability that more than $\ell/3$ rounds returned $\bot$ is at most $\binom{\ell}{\ell/3}(1/\log(8t))^{\ell/3}\leq(8/\log(8t))^{\ell/3}\leq 1/t^{2}$ . ∎

#### Claim 5.7.

With at least $1-1/t^{0.9}$ probability, for all $r\in[\ell]$ , either $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}=\bot$ or $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}=\hat{C}^{(r)}$ .

#### Proof.

By the second bullet point of Lemma 5.1, for each round $r$ , the probability that $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}\neq\bot$ and $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}\neq\hat{C}^{(r)}$ is at most $1/(8t)$ . The claim then follows from a union bound over $\ell=\lceil 10\log t/\log\log t\rceil$ rounds. ∎

Now we analyze the correctness of our algorithm. Since we return $\bot$ only if more than $\ell/3$ rounds returned $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}=\bot$ , the first bullet point in the lemma statement immediately follows from Claim 5.6.

Now we prove the second bullet point. We assume the events in Claim 5.5 and Claim 5.7 both happen (which holds with at least $1-1/t^{0.9}-1/t^{18}\geq 1-1/\sqrt{t}$ probability by a union bound). We also assume $\leq\ell/3$ of the rounds returned $\bot$ (otherwise, our algorithm would return $\bot$ in the end, and there is nothing to prove). In this case, for every $k\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ , by Claim 5.5 there are at least $\ell/2$ rounds $r$ with $\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+2p]+\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+3p]\neq 0$ , among which there are only $<\ell/3$ rounds with $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}=\bot$ , and the remaining $\ell/2-\ell/3\geq 1$ non- $\bot$ rounds must satisfy $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}[k+2p]+\widetilde{C}^{(r)}[k+3p]=\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+2p]+\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+3p]\neq 0$ by Claim 5.7, and thus $k$ is included in our returned set Eq. 11. For every $k\in[p]\setminus\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star_{p}B)$ , we know $\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+2p]+\hat{C}^{(r)}[k+3p]=0$ always holds, and then by Claim 5.7 we know $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}[k+2p]+\widetilde{C}^{(r)}[k+3p]=0$ holds whenever $\widetilde{C}^{(r)}\neq\bot$ , and hence $k$ is not included in our returned set Eq. 11. This finishes the proof of the second bullet point. ∎

### 5.2 Sparse nonnegative convolution with high success probability

Now we will use Lemma 5.2 and Lemma 5.4 to boost Lemma 4.3 to succeed with high probability.

Recall that in the proof of Lemma 4.3 we sample a random $p\leq t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ to reduce the length of the input vectors to $t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ while incurring $\leq t/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ collisions in expectation. In the following, we use Lemma 5.2 to find a prime $p$ that incurs $\leq t/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ collisions with high probability.

#### Lemma 5.8 (Finding a good $p$ w.h.p.).

Let $t$ be a parameter, $A,B\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ be input vectors with $\|A\|_{0},\|B\|_{0}\leq t$ , and $N\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ . There is a randomized algorithm that outputs a prime $p\leq t\log^{5}t$ in (worst case) $O(t\log t)$ time, such that: If $\|A\star B\|_{0}\leq t$ , then with at least $1-1/t^{0.3}$ probability,

$$ |\{k\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B):\text{exists }k^{\prime}\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)\setminus\{k\}\text{ s.t. }k^{\prime}\equiv_{p}k\}|\leq O\big(\tfrac{t}{\log^{3}t}\big). $$

#### Proof.

Denote the left hand side of Eq. 12 by $f_{p}$ . We have the following bound on $f_{p}$ over a random prime $p$ .

#### Claim 5.9.

Suppose $\|A\star B\|_{0}\leq t$ . Then, for a uniform random prime $p\in[0.5t\log^{5}t,t\log^{5}t]$ , we have $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p}[f_{p}\leq\frac{ct}{\log^{3}t}]\geq 1-\frac{1}{\log t}$ for some constant $c>0$ .

#### Proof.

For each $0\leq k<k^{\prime}\leq 2N-2\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ we have $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p}[p\mid k^{\prime}-k]\leq\frac{\log 2N/\log(0.5t\log^{5}t)}{\Omega(t\log^{5}t/\log(t\log^{5}t))}=O(\frac{1}{t\log^{4}t})$ by the prime number theorem (similarly to Footnote 2). Then, for each $k\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ , by a union bound, the probability that there exists $k^{\prime}\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)\setminus\{k\}$ with $k^{\prime}\equiv_{p}k$ is at most $\|A\star B\|_{0}\cdot O(\frac{1}{t\log^{4}t})\leq O(\frac{1}{\log^{4}t})$ . By linearity of expectation, we know $\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{p}[f_{p}]\leq O(\frac{t}{\log^{4}t})$ . By Markov’s inequality, we know $f_{p}\leq ct/\log^{3}t$ holds with at least $1-1/\log t$ probability where $c$ is some constant. ∎

We can relate $f_{p}$ with $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}$ via the following property

$$ \frac{f_{p}}{2}\leq\|A\star B\|_{0}-\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}\leq f_{p}. $$

To show Eq. 13, consider bucketing $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ modulo $p$ , and observe that each non-empty bucket of size $x$ ( $x\geq 1$ ) contributes $x-1$ to the quantity $\|A\star B\|_{0}-\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}$ and contributes $x\cdot\mathbf{1}[x\geq 2]$ to $f_{p}$ , and use the inequality $\frac{1}{2}x\cdot\mathbf{1}[x\geq 2]\leq x-1\leq x\cdot\mathbf{1}[x\geq 2]$ to get Eq. 13.

Informally speaking, our plan is as follows: Claim 5.9 means that a random sample of $O(\log t/\log\log t)$ primes $p$ will contain a good prime with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ probability, and our goal is to efficiently find a good prime among these sampled primes. To do this, we will use Lemma 5.2 to estimate the size of $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}$ for each sampled prime $p$ , and keep the prime $p$ that (approximately) maximizes $\|A\star_{p}B\|_{0}$ (which means small $f_{p}$ by Eq. 13).

In more detail, our algorithm works as follows:

For $r=1,2,\dots,\ell:=\lceil 5\log t/\log\log t\rceil$ :

- • Sample a uniform random prime $p_{r}\in[0.5t\log^{5}t,t\log^{5}t]$ . Let $\widetilde{A}:=h(A),\widetilde{B}=h(B)\in\mathbb{N}^{p_{r}}$ where $h(x)=x\bmod p_{r}$ .

- • Repeatedly run the algorithm from Lemma 5.2 on $\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B}\in\mathbb{N}^{p_{r}}$ with parameter $t$ , until the output is not $\bot$ . Denote the output integer by $\widetilde{g}_{p_{r}}$ .

Finally, return the prime $p_{r^{*}}$ with maximum $\widetilde{g}_{p_{r^{*}}}$ .

If the algorithm runs for longer than $O(t\log t)$ time, then we abort and output an arbitrary prime.

We first analyze the running time of the algorithm described above.

#### Claim 5.10.

The algorithm described above (without aborting) finishes in time $O(t\log t)$ with at least $1-1/t$ probability.

#### Proof.

It is easy to see that the total time for generating $\ell$ primes is $\ell\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)\leq\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ with probability $1-1/t^{100}$ , and is negligible. In the following we focus on the inner for-loop that invokes Lemma 5.2.

Each call of Lemma 5.2 returns $\bot$ with only $\leq 1/\log t$ probability. Since our algorithm runs the inner for-loop $\ell$ times, we need $\ell$ calls of Lemma 5.2 to return non- $\bot$ in order for our algorithm to finish (before being aborted). Among the first (up to) $2\ell$ calls of Lemma 5.2 made by the algorithm, the probability that only $<\ell$ of these calls returned non- $\bot$ can be bounded by $\binom{2\ell}{2\ell-\ell}\cdot(1/\log t)^{2\ell-\ell}\leq(4/\log t)^{\ell}\leq t^{-2}$ . Hence, with $1-t^{-2}$ probability, the total time for the inner for-loop is at most $\ell\cdot O(t\log\log t)\leq O(t\log t)$ .

In summary, our algorithm finishes in $O(t\log t)$ time (without being aborted) with $1-t^{-100}-t^{-2}\geq 1-1/t$ probability. ∎

Now we analyze the correctness of the algorithm. We only need to consider the $\|A\star B\|_{0}\leq t$ case. Lemma 5.2 guarantees that each $\widetilde{g}_{p_{r}}$ is correct with probability $\geq 1-1/\sqrt{t}$ , where being correct means differing from $\|\widetilde{A}\star_{p_{r}}\widetilde{B}\|_{0}=\|A\star_{p_{r}}B\|_{0}$ by at most an additive $\sqrt{\|\widetilde{A}\star_{p_{r}}\widetilde{B}\|_{0}}t^{0.4}\leq\sqrt{\|A\star B\|_{0}}t^{0.4}\leq t^{0.9}$ . By a union bound over the first (up to) $2\ell$ calls of Lemma 5.2 (which we know is sufficient by the proof of Claim 5.10), all $\widetilde{g}_{p_{r}}$ are correct with probability at least $1-2\ell/\sqrt{t}\geq 1-1/t^{0.4}$ . In this case, the final $p_{r^{*}}$ returned by our algorithm, which maximizes $\widetilde{g}_{p_{r^{*}}}$ , should also approximately maximize $\|A\star_{p_{r^{*}}}B\|_{0}$ , i.e.,

$$ \|A\star_{p_{r^{*}}}B\|_{0}\geq\|A\star_{p_{r}}B\|_{0}-2t^{0.9}\text{ for all $1\leq r\leq\ell$.} $$

On the other hand, by Claim 5.9, we know with at least $1-(1/\log t)^{\ell}\geq 1-1/t^{5}$ probability, there is some sampled prime $p_{r}$ $(1\leq r\leq\ell)$ such that $f_{p_{r}}\leq\frac{ct}{\log^{3}t}$ . Combine this with Eq. 14 and Eq. 13, and we get

$$ \displaystyle f_{p_{r^{*}}} \displaystyle\leq 2(\|A\star B\|_{0}-\|A\star_{p_{r^{*}}}B\|_{0}) \displaystyle\leq 2(\|A\star B\|_{0}-\|A\star_{p_{r}}B\|_{0}+2t^{0.9}) \displaystyle\leq 2(f_{p_{r}}+2t^{0.9}) \displaystyle\leq 2(\tfrac{ct}{\log^{3}t}+2t^{0.9}) \displaystyle\leq\tfrac{6ct}{\log^{3}t}, $$

which means the prime $p_{r^{*}}$ found by our algorithm indeed satisfies the desired property. Finally we apply a union bound over all the bad events mentioned earlier. The probability that the algorithm fails to run within time $O(t\log t)$ is $\leq 1/t$ by Claim 5.10, the probability some call of Lemma 5.2 fails is $\leq 1/t^{0.4}$ , and the probability that none of the sampled primes $p_{r}$ has $f_{p_{r}}\leq\frac{ct}{\log^{3}t}$ is $\leq 1/t^{5}$ . Hence, the overall error probability is $\leq 1/t+1/t^{0.4}+1/t^{5}\leq 1/t^{0.3}$ for sufficiently large $t$ . This finishes the proof of Lemma 5.8. ∎

Finally, we are ready to prove the main theorem, under Assumption 1 (which is required by Lemma 4.2).

#### Proof.

By the length reduction step of Lemma 4.5, it suffices to solve the case where $N\leq(\|A\|_{0}\|B\|_{0})^{3}$ . Recall that in the nonnegative setting we have $t=\|A\star B\|_{0}\in[\max\{\|A\|_{0},\|B\|_{0}\},\|A\|_{0}\cdot\|B\|_{0}]$ .

In the following, we describe a Las Vegas algorithm that solves the problem with the following guarantee: it runs in worst-case $O(t\log t)$ time, and either outputs the correct result or outputs $\bot$ , and the probability of outputting $\bot$ is at most $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ .

- 1. We first apply the algorithm from Lemma 2.15 to $X=\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A),Y=\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(B)$ and $\delta=1/(\|A\|_{0}+\|B\|_{0})^{2}\leq 1/t$ , to obtain an approximation $t^{*}$ that always satisfies $t^{*}\leq O(t)$ , and satisfies $t\leq t^{*}$ with $1-\delta\geq 1-1/t$ probability. The running time is $O(t\log(1/\delta)+t\log\log t)=O(t\log t)$ .

- 2. Then, we run Lemma 5.8 (using parameter $t^{*}$ ) to find a good hash function $h(x)=x\bmod{p}$ where $p\leq t\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(t)$ , in $O(t\log t)$ time. Assuming the estimate $t^{*}$ from the previous step is successful (i.e., $t\leq t^{*}$ ), with at least $1-1/t^{0.3}$ success probability it holds that hashing $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(A\star B)$ to $[p]$ only incurs $O(t/\log^{3}t)$ collisions.

- 3. Then, we run Lemma 5.4 (using parameter $t^{*}$ ) to compute $S=\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(h(A)\star_{p}h(B))$ in $O(t\log t)$ time. If Lemma 5.4 returns $\bot$ , then we terminate the algorithm and return $\bot$ . By Lemma 5.4, assuming the estimate $t^{*}$ from the first step is successful, the probability of returning $\bot$ is at most $1/t^{2}$ . Moreover, Lemma 5.4 states that the probability of computing an incorrect (and non- $\bot$ ) $S$ is at most $1/t^{0.5}$ .

- 4. Using the set $S$ computed by the previous step, we run Lemma 4.2 to compute $h(A)\star_{p}h(B)$ , $h(\partial A)\star_{p}h(B)+h(A)\star_{p}h(\partial B)$ and $h(\partial^{2}A)\star_{p}h(B)+2h(\partial A)\star_{p}h(\partial B)+h(A)\star_{p}h(\partial^{2}B)$ , in $O(t\log t)$ time. By the guarantee of Lemma 4.2, either these vectors are computed correctly, or Lemma 4.2 returns $\bot$ at least once, in which case we also terminate the algorithm and return $\bot$ . Moreover, if the support $S$ computed by the previous step is correct, then the probability of returning $\bot$ is at most $O(1/t)$ .

- 5. Given $h(A)\star_{p}h(B)$ , $h(\partial A)\star_{p}h(B)+h(A)\star_{p}h(\partial B)$ and $h(\partial^{2}A)\star_{p}h(B)+2h(\partial A)\star_{p}h(\partial B)+h(A)\star_{p}h(\partial^{2}B)$ computed by the previous step (which must be correct, if the algorithm reaches this step), we use the same method as in the proof of Lemma 4.3 to recover all the entries in $A\star B$ that do not have collisions using the hash function $h(x)=x\bmod p$ . Moreover, if $\|A\star B-C\|_{0}\leq O(t/\log^{3}t)$ holds, then $R+C=A\star B$ holds with $1-1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ probability. We return $R+C$ as the answer if it passes the check $\|R+C\|_{1}=\|A\|_{1}\|B\|_{1}$ , and return $\bot$ otherwise.

By the discussion above, it is clear that the algorithm either returns the correct answer $A\star B$ or returns $\bot$ . Moreover, by a union bound over all the steps, the probability of returning $\bot$ can be bounded by $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ .

The main theorem directly follows from running a constant number of repetitions of this Las Vegas algorithm to reduce the overall failure probability from $1/\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(t)$ to $1/t$ . ∎

### 5.3 Proof of Lemma 5.1

In this section we prove Lemma 5.1 using techniques from [20], Prony’s method with bit packing (Lemma 2.12), as well as some other tricks.

One of the key ingredients in the work of Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos [20] is an (almost) 3-wise independence result of the hash family $h(x)=((\sigma x+\tau)\bmod p)\bmod m$ , which improved an earlier result of Knudsen [62] in some specific regime of interest. We will use this result in the same way as in [20] to analyze the number of elements hashed to heavy buckets.

#### Definition 5.11 (Almost linear hash family $h$ ).

Let $p$ be a fixed prime, and $m\leq p$ be the number of buckets. Let $\sigma,\tau\in[p]$ be chosen uniformly and independently at random, and define the hash function $h(x):=\pi(x)\bmod m$ , where $\pi(x):=(\sigma x+\tau)\bmod p$ .

#### Lemma 5.12 (Overfull buckets, follows from [20]).

Let $X\subseteq[N]$ be a set of keys, and let $t\geq|X|$ . Randomly pick a hash function $h(x)=\pi(x)\bmod m$ from Definition 5.11 with parameters $p>4N^{2}$ and $m\leq N$ . Let $\widetilde{X}:=\pi(X)+\{0,p\}$ . Then, with at least $1-O(1/\log^{2}N)$ probability, it holds that

$$ \Big\lvert\Big\{y\in\widetilde{X}:\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\widetilde{X}}\mathbf{1}\left[y\equiv y^{\prime}\pmod{m}\right]>\frac{4t}{m}\Big\}\Big\rvert\leq\frac{mN\log^{3}N}{t}. $$

Eq. 15 follows from [20, Corollary 11.3, Lemma 5.5] with a slight change of parameters. We redo the calculation and prove Eq. 15 in Section B.4.
